client: I've been really struggling since my grandma passed away last month. Every time my family gets together now, I just feel this heavy emptiness where she should be. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help - the pain feels too deep.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a profound sense of loss, especially during family gatherings where your grandma's absence feels so present. I notice you're questioning whether talking about it will help—what comes up when you consider sharing more about how you're feeling? Sometimes, even naming the pain can create space to process it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I don't know...every time I try to talk about her, I just feel this lump in my throat and then I shut down. Part of me worries that if I start crying, I'll never stop. And honestly, sometimes it feels like talking about it just makes the pain worse instead of better. 

My family has this unspoken rule where we don't mention her at gatherings anymore, like we're all pretending it's fine. But then I see her empty chair at the dinner table and it's like this huge elephant in the room that nobody acknowledges.
therapist: I hear how painful it is when words get stuck in your throat while everyone around you stays silent—it sounds like you're grieving both your grandma and the way your family avoids acknowledging this loss. Your voice sounds like it's carrying a lot of energy when you describe this, even as the words themselves feel heavy—would it feel safe to explore what might happen if you did let those tears out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if crying would help. Every time I start to feel it coming, I just freeze up—like if I start, I'll lose control completely. Plus, my family would just get uncomfortable if they saw me crying. They'd probably tell me to "be strong" like they always do.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding back not just from the grief itself, but also from the fear of how others might react to your pain—that "be strong" message seems to have created a lot of pressure. I notice your voice speeds up when you talk about freezing up—what does that moment of holding back feel like in your body?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It feels like my chest gets tight and my throat closes up—like if I start crying, I won't be able to stop. I hate that feeling because it makes me feel weak, even though logically I know grief isn't weakness. But what if people see me break down and think I'm being dramatic or attention-seeking? That fear keeps me frozen.
therapist: You're describing such a painful conflict—knowing grief isn't weakness intellectually, yet feeling terrified that others might judge your emotions as exactly that. That tightness in your chest sounds like your body trying to protect you from both the grief and those fears of being seen as "too much"—would it help to explore what "being strong" might look like if it included space for these feelings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... the idea of "being strong" while also showing emotions just feels impossible right now. Whenever I've tried to open up before, people either give me empty platitudes or change the subject awkwardly. It makes me feel even more alone, like my grief is something to be fixed quickly rather than just felt. 

That tightness in my chest gets worse when I think about trying this "space for feelings" approach - what if it just makes me fall apart completely? I've spent years building up this controlled exterior, and the thought of dismantling it is terrifying.
therapist: It sounds like past experiences of opening up have left you feeling dismissed, making the idea of creating space for these emotions feel more like risking collapse than healing. Your rapid, soft-spoken way of describing this tells me how vulnerable this fear feels—what would need to be different for that tightness to ease, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if anything could make it feel safe to open up again. Last time I tried being vulnerable with my friend, they just changed the subject like my feelings were inconvenient. Now whenever I start to share something personal, my chest gets this heavy, panicky feeling like I'm making a mistake.
therapist: That panicky feeling in your chest seems to be carrying both the grief and the memory of being dismissed—it makes complete sense that you'd hesitate to open up again after that experience. I hear how carefully you're weighing the risks of vulnerability—what do you imagine might happen if someone actually stayed present with your feelings instead of changing the subject?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don’t know, the idea of someone actually staying present with my feelings almost scares me more than being dismissed. What if they see how messy I really am and walk away? At least when people change the subject, I can tell myself they just didn’t get it, not that I’m too much to handle.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two painful fears—being misunderstood or being truly seen in your messiness. Your voice rises with urgency as you describe this dilemma—what would it feel like to imagine someone who could handle both seeing you fully and choosing to stay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
That sounds so impossible right now. I guess part of me wants to believe someone could handle seeing the messy parts, but the other part is convinced they'd just walk away. I've had people leave before when things got difficult, so why would this time be any different? 

Even the idea of imagining that kind of person makes my chest feel tight. Like I'm setting myself up to be disappointed again.
therapist: Your voice speeds up when you talk about past disappointments—it sounds like those experiences left deep marks that make hope feel risky right now. That tightness in your chest seems to be holding both the longing for connection and the fear of being let down again—what’s it like to notice those two feelings existing together?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: It's exhausting holding both those feelings at once. Part of me still wants to reach out to people, but then I remember all the times I've been ghosted or rejected and just... shut down. It's like my body physically braces for disappointment before anything even happens.
therapist: It sounds like that exhaustion comes from carrying both the desire to connect and the anticipation of rejection—like your body is preparing to protect you before anything even happens. What’s it like to notice that pattern of bracing yourself, even as part of you still wants to reach out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
It's exhausting to feel this way all the time. Like I'm constantly torn between wanting friends and being convinced they'll eventually reject me anyway. I don't even know how to stop bracing for impact—it feels automatic now. 

Sometimes I wonder if I'm just making it worse by expecting the worst, but then I think "well at least I won't be surprised when it happens." It's messed up.
therapist: You're describing such a painful cycle—wanting connection while preparing for rejection, almost as if you're trying to soften the blow before it even comes. That automatic bracing seems to have become its own kind of protection—what do you think might shift if you could notice that pattern without judging yourself for it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech
